"We are closing the schools to slow transmission" of sickness, he said. Bloomberg, flanked by New York Gov. Bloomberg indicated the school administrator had a pre-existing medical condition. Fifty students at that school have been sent home with flu-like symptoms since May 6. At the two other schools, the primary school had an overflowing nurse's office Thursday, reporting 29 students suffering from flu-like symptoms. The other intermediate school had 241 students absent with illness Thursday. The New York City Department of Health and the Department of Education have been in nearly constant contact, said Jason Post, a spokesman from Bloomberg's office. When there's a spike in students absent from classes, the Department of Health is alerted. "There's always good communication, flu or no flu," Post said. "But our senses have been sharp for a while now." The Health Department has seen a general increase in flu activity in Queens, officials said in a news release. While the symptoms of H1N1 flu seem to resemble those of seasonal flu, the H1N1 virus appears to spread more extensively, at least in schools, warranting closures to slow transmission in the community, the release said. Dr. Isaac Weisfuse, the deputy commissioner of the city's Department of Hygiene and Mental Health, said although concern is legitimate, there's no solid evidence that suggests the H1N1 flu -- also known as swine flu -- is more dangerous than the flu in general. "The bottom line is if you're sick, stay home," Weisfuse said. "And don't go back to school until you're better for one whole day." In late April, St. Francis Prep, a high school in Queens, was closed because of a flu outbreak. Since then, the school reopened and the stricken students have recovered, according to the mayor's office. "As we have said from the outset of the appearance of H1N1 in our city last month, we will share with New Yorkers what we know and not speculate on what we don't know," said Bloomberg in a statement. According to the World Health Organization and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, as of Thursday night 7,412 cases of H1N1 flu have been confirmed worldwide. The organizations said 63 deaths attributed to the virus have been confirmed worldwide. The CDC said 4,298 cases of the virus and three fatalities have been confirmed in the United States as of Thursday night. New York had 224 confirmed cases of H1N1, the CDC said. It was not clear whether the five cases cited by Bloomberg and the other New York officials were included in the latest CDC total.

The decision affects Intermediate School 238, Public School 16, and Intermediate School 5, all located in Queens. City health officials reported that hundreds of students across the three facilities had stayed home in recent days displaying high fevers, severe coughs, and other symptoms associated with the H1N1 virus.

"Our top priority is the health and safety of our children, our teachers, and our school staff," Bloomberg said during a press conference at City Hall. "While we still believe this virus is generally mild in most cases, the sheer volume of absent students in these specific schools warrants a temporary closure to stop the chain of transmission."

The closures come as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reported Thursday that confirmed and probable H1N1 cases in the United States have topped 4,700 across 47 states, with 173 total hospitalizations and four recorded deaths nationwide. 

New York State has emerged as one of the national hotspots, with more than 200 confirmed cases—the vast majority of them centered in New York City. CDC director Dr. Richard Besser noted in a morning briefing that while the national picture suggests the virus is not currently as deadly as initially feared in late April, "localized clusters" like the one in Queens present unique public health challenges.

NYC Health Commissioner Dr. Thomas Frieden, who was recently tapped by President Barack Obama to take over the CDC later this summer, stressed that the school closures were a targeted measure rather than a citywide directive.

"We are not seeing a widespread, severe outbreak across all five boroughs, but we are seeing unusually high flu activity in specific pockets of Queens," Dr. Frieden said. "Closing these three schools allows us to break the cycle of infection while we monitor the situation closely."

Education Chancellor Joel Klein said the city would conduct a deep cleaning and disinfection of all three school buildings before students are allowed to return. Remote learning packages are being prepared for affected families, though officials acknowledged the abrupt disruption to working parents.

Outside I.S. 238 in Hollis, Queens, parents expressed a mixture of relief and anxiety as they picked up homework packets on Thursday afternoon.

"I think closing the school is the right call," said Maria Gonzales, whose 12-year-old son attends I.S. 238. "Half his class was missing yesterday. You just don't want to take any chances when it comes to a new virus."

City officials said one school staff member—an assistant principal at I.S. 238—is currently hospitalized in critical condition with flu symptoms, escalating concerns among local residents and teachers' union leaders.

Mayor Bloomberg urged New Yorkers not to panic, reminding the public to practice basic hygiene measures like frequent handwashing and staying home when sick. 

"We have been planning for public health emergencies for years," Bloomberg said. "The city's health system is strong, our response is calibrated to the facts on the ground, and we will get through this."

**As H1N1 Flu Spreads Through NYC Classrooms, Fear and Policy Shift Test Nation’s Largest School District**

**NEW YORK — May 20, 2009** — What began weeks ago as a cluster of mild, flu-like symptoms among students returning from spring break at a Queens high school has metastasized into the biggest public health challenge for New York City’s school system in decades. 

As the new H1N1 influenza virus—commonly known as swine flu—sweeps through the five boroughs, school attendance has plummeted, dozens of school buildings have been temporarily shuttered, and city officials are grappling with how to contain a novel virus without shutting down the nation’s largest educational network.

The epicenter of the New York outbreak was St. Francis Preparatory School in Fresh Meadows, Queens. In late April, dozens of students suddenly came down with high fevers, sore throats, and body aches following a popular spring break trip to Cancun, Mexico. Within days, the virus spread beyond the private Catholic school and into the public system, jumping from neighborhood to neighborhood.

Panic reached a peak earlier this week following the tragic death of Mitchell Wiener, a 55-year-old assistant principal at Intermediate School 238 in Hollis, Queens. Wiener, a beloved educator who had worked in the school system for nearly three decades, succumbed to complications from the H1N1 virus on Sunday. His death transformed what many had viewed as a minor health nuisance into a sobering reality.

"This is a heartbreaking reminder that while this virus is mild for the vast majority of people, it can be extraordinarily dangerous for some," Mayor Michael Bloomberg said at a press conference outside City Hall, where he urged calm while emphasizing vigilance. 

In the days following Wiener’s hospitalization, fear rippled through the city. Outside schools across Brooklyn and Queens, parents assembled in the morning cool to anxiously debate whether to send their children inside. Hand sanitizer bottles, once a rarity in school halls, have become ubiquitous, and school nurses are reporting overwhelming lines of students complaining of coughs and chills.

To date, the Department of Education has temporarily closed more than 30 public and private schools in an effort to break the chain of transmission. However, the closures have created a secondary crisis for low-income families who rely on schools not just for education, but for childcare and free meals.

The rapidly evolving situation has forced health officials to adjust their strategy on the fly. Initially, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommended shutting down any school with a confirmed H1N1 case. But with the virus now spreading through community transmission, city health officials argue that wide-scale school closures do little to stop the flu while causing massive disruption to working parents.

"We cannot close every school where the flu appears," said New York City Health Commissioner Dr. Thomas Farley, who recently succeeded Dr. Thomas Frieden after Frieden was tapped to head the CDC. "If a virus is widespread in the community, closing a school just means children will interact in park playgrounds or at home instead of in classrooms. Our focus must shift from stopping the virus entirely to protecting those most vulnerable to severe illness."

Under the city’s revised guidelines, schools will only be closed if there is a dramatic surge in flu-like illnesses accompanied by a high concentration of high-risk students, such as those with severe asthma or compromised immune systems. Otherwise, the guidance to parents remains simple: keep sick children home for at least seven days, or until they have been fever-free for 24 hours without medication.

Despite the official reassurances, attendance in affected districts has dropped significantly, with some schools reporting up to 40 percent absenteeism. Teachers are attempting to balance remote lesson planning for absent students while managing half-empty classrooms.

"It’s surreal," said Maria Santos, a sixth-grade teacher at a middle school in the South Bronx. "Half my class is gone. The kids who are here are constantly washing their hands, and every time someone coughs, the whole room goes silent."

As summer approaches, health authorities hope the warmer weather will slow the spread of the virus, granting a temporary reprieve. However, global health officials are warning that H1N1 could return with a vengeance in the autumn. 

City officials are already preparing for a massive fall vaccination campaign, pending the development and distribution of an H1N1-specific vaccine. For now, New York City's 1.1 million school children and their families are left navigating a tense finish to the school year, learning to live with an invisible threat that has reshaped daily life in the classroom.

#### Health Officials Pivot Strategy

Speaking at a news conference on Thursday, Dr. Isaac Weisfuse, New York City’s Deputy Health Commissioner for Disease Control, addressed the growing unease among parents and school personnel while outlining the city's targeted intervention strategy.

According to the latest data released by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), confirmed and probable cases of H1N1 in the United States have surpassed 4,250 across 47 states, resulting in more than 110 hospitalizations and three confirmed fatalities nationwide. #### Guidance for Parents and the Public

City health officials urge parents of students attending the closed Queens schools to keep their children at home and avoid large public gatherings during the five-day closure. Dr. Weisfuse urged residents to practice standard preventative hygiene, including frequent handwashing and staying home at the onset of flu-like symptoms.
